text: The power-range channels use ion-chamber detector current signals. The upper and lower detector outputs are combined to form a channel power signal, and detector outputs are compared to provide power-distribution information and check relative calibration.

The document describes power-range neutron-flux leakage detection using independent ionization-chamber current signals. It states that individual detector currents are monitored and that the summed channel signal is proportional to neutron flux for the associated core quadrant.

section_path: 2.3 Physical and Mathematical Basis of Core Monitoring
text: For periodically read detector currents, the text recommends comparing a current value with its preceding value and filtering changes associated with electronic contact or operation error. It also notes that time variation may be compared with other detectors in the same detector chain.

For surveillance or monitoring, the document describes measuring induced noise, typically neutron noise, and identifying anomalies from signatures in the measured spectra. It distinguishes this from quantitative localization or strength estimation, which additionally requires an appropriate transfer function.

The document defines direct diagnostics as direct measurement of a process time series to classify whether it reflects normal or abnormal behaviour, without trying to identify the anomaly cause or underlying physical process.

For high-quality, high-frequency reactor-noise analysis, the document states that sampling rate, amplitude resolution, conditioning, isolation, simultaneous sampling and synchronization requirements are commonly more stringent than those of a typical plant computer or historian.

The document notes that a self-powered flux detector can produce an analogue current signal in the microampere range. For current signals, the acquisition path needs current-to-voltage conversion before subsequent signal conditioning and simultaneous multichannel ADC sampling.

The document states that many noise measurements are made during steady-state high-power operation without operator-induced changes when establishing signature baselines or detecting anomalies. Measurements taken during operating-mode changes are described as transient-response measurements rather than traditional noise measurements.

section_path: Pattern Definition and Normal Reference Data
text: The HFIR study formed normal-reference data from records gathered during normal operation, where normality had been independently determined by examining reactor mechanical integrity. It then used subcategories of that reference data to identify observations deviating from the normal patterns.

The HFIR study reports that sampling must be adequate to characterize reactor operational status and that a spectral feature may be normal at one fuel-cycle phase but not at another. It therefore recommends time-varying reference templates for different operating phases.

The review states that in-core and excore neutron instrumentation supports neutron-flux monitoring, and that fission chambers and self-powered neutron detectors can provide instantaneous data for detailed reactor monitoring.

The review distinguishes pulse, Campbell, and current operating modes for fission chambers. In current mode, collected charge is integrated to an average current proportional to fission rate and neutron flux, while gamma contribution can be significant at high flux.

The Campbell mode uses the variance or mean square of detector current and is intended for an intermediate flux regime; its weighting suppresses gamma-induced contribution relative to neutron-induced contribution.
For high-temperature fission chambers, the review identifies insulation-resistance loss, leak current, and partial discharges under bias as mechanisms that can perturb the measurement signal.

The review explains that delayed self-powered neutron detectors produce a measurable external current from beta emission after neutron capture. Typical current is a few microamperes at the cited thermal-flux condition, and response time is on the order of minutes depending on emitter half-life.

Prompt self-powered neutron detectors can have quasi-instantaneous response, but the review notes lower neutron efficiency and a higher relative contribution from external gamma rays than for delayed detectors.
The review reports that an in-core SPND signal can provide dynamic information on neutron-flux perturbations in the cited application, after considering the relevant gamma contribution.

The review notes that gamma-induced SPND current is typically lower than neutron-induced current under the cited neutron-to-gamma conditions, but gamma sensitivity depends strongly on detector surroundings and gamma spectrum.

The review describes response-function compensation for delayed SPNDs as a route to real-time neutron-flux information and notes state-space processing and Kalman filtering as candidate processing approaches.

The review reports that detector surroundings and materials can perturb vanadium SPND signals, including contributions attributed to fission betas, activated structures, and dissolved hydrogen; the cited effects were not observed for rhodium SPNDs.
In the cited prototype tests, SPND responses were verified as proportional to reactor power, prompt and delayed contributions were quantified, and gamma contributions were experimentally determined.

section_path: 5.1 PWR Neutron Noise Data from Ex-Core Detectors
text: The PWR study records ex-core power-range monitor data and reduces it to frequency-domain spectra. It states that sampling rate, block size, and averaged-block count determine frequency resolution, analysis bandwidth, and the variance of spectral estimates.

section_path: 5.1 PWR Neutron Noise Data from Ex-Core Detectors
text: For low-frequency neutron-spectrum analysis, the study selected a long recording obtained under steady-state 100% power and flow conditions. It separately used shorter full-power/full-flow recordings for mechanical-model analysis across the surveillance period.

The study describes automated surveillance of dynamic reactor signals by statistically comparing current neutron power-spectral-density measurements with past baseline PSDs from the same reactor system.
The study states that a surveillance comparison uses a reference PSD representing the baseline condition for the current operational state, and stores detected changes for later diagnostic analysis.
The cited surveillance discriminants are designed to identify integral spectral-power changes, narrow-band magnitude changes, spectral-shape changes, and spectral-peak frequency shifts.

The study notes that a squared log-ratio spectral discriminator avoids cancellation of opposite deviations but loses the direction of a spectral shift. It therefore uses complementary discriminators and updates confidence intervals during a learning phase using measured statistics.
The study cautions that an offline sensitivity comparison without ongoing confidence-interval updating is limited by assumptions about the original measured signal.

The source-range channel conditions neutron pulse signals through amplification, shaping, integration, gamma/background discrimination, and logarithmic signal generation. The document identifies neutron/gamma discrimination as particularly important when neutron flux is low and gamma field is high.

The intermediate-range system uses two independent channels and compensated ion-chamber signals proportional to neutron flux. A logarithmic current-measuring circuit monitors power across eight decades and provides both flux level and rate-of-change indications.
The document describes source-range detector pulses being preamplified near the detector to improve signal-to-noise ratio, with provision for known self-test frequencies in the preamplifier chain.

In the source-range channel, adjustable amplification and discrimination separate neutron pulses from lower-amplitude gamma-generated pulses; the conditioned pulse train is integrated to a current proportional to logarithm of average pulse rate.

The source-range description notes that intentional high-voltage removal during startup is annunciated differently from a voltage fault, and that inserted test signals are additive to the detector signal.

The intermediate-range system uses compensated ion chambers with high-voltage and compensating-voltage supplies. The compensating voltage cancels gamma contribution to the total current, and the logarithmic amplifier produces an analogue output proportional to logarithm of input current.

The intermediate-range description provides separate alarms for detector and compensating-voltage loss and specifies that test signals are injected at the logarithmic-amplifier input under a trip-bypass interlock.

The power-range description states that each dual-section ion chamber provides upper and lower neutron-current signals proportional to core-quadrant flux. The individual signals are displayed, isolated, and combined into a linear channel signal proportional to the associated neutron flux.

The power-range rate circuit compares actual power with a delayed power signal and produces trips for sufficiently high positive or negative rate. The document states that its setpoints are selected so normal design transients do not actuate these rate trips.

IAEA describes neutron-flux measurements as serving reactivity, power control, shutdown, and core-diagnostic functions. It distinguishes external detectors for global or regional flux from in-core detectors for localized flux and identifies fission chambers, ion chambers, and SPNDs as detector types.

The IAEA text describes source, intermediate, and power measurement ranges, their detector types, gamma compensation in intermediate range, and pulse versus low-level steady-current outputs. It notes near-detector conversion/amplification and separate filtered versus unfiltered paths for average flux and noise diagnostics.

The text distinguishes a field sensor from transmitter electronics and states that a conventional analogue transmitter can provide a calibrated current output over a specified process-variable span; suppressed zero can reveal an open circuit.
The text notes that smart transmitters may provide self-diagnosis, signal validation, remote parameter reset, recalibration, and calibration checking in addition to analogue or digital outputs.

The IAEA text identifies current-to-voltage conversion, gain matching, isolation, DC removal, anti-aliasing, and multiplexer phase shifts as relevant data-acquisition considerations. It notes that separate simultaneously triggered ADCs avoid multiplexer-induced phase concerns.

For neutronics-noise and other high-speed monitoring, the document describes high-resolution delta-sigma ADC use and notes that control-module prioritization and communication integrity are necessary to avoid lost or corrupted data.
The text identifies long-term archival accessibility as a data-acquisition concern and requires isolation of safety signals when installing permanent or temporary diagnostic data-acquisition systems.

The APRM description combines inputs from multiple local power range monitors distributed axially and radially. It notes that average-power channel response is less uniform near control-rod movement because local detector changes can be larger.
The APRM count circuit assesses whether enough LPRM inputs are operable for adequate average-power representation, explicitly accounting for low-range readings that can be zero or near zero.
The APRM averaging circuit uses only operational LPRM signals and is periodically adjusted against a heat-balance power reference between periodic calibrations.
The APRM thermal trip averages power over approximately six seconds and therefore filters short high-magnitude spikes, while the fixed neutron trip protects those short events.

section_path: 5.4.2.5.6 APRM Flow Bias Not Normal Trip
text: The APRM flow-bias function compares independently calculated recirculation-flow values and uses a mismatch criterion to trigger a rod block in the documented design.

The ORNL study frames neutron-noise work as recording available detector and process signals, reducing them to noise signatures, and documenting relationships among spatially separated neutron detectors and process variables before model-based interpretation.

The study describes LPRM strings containing axially distributed fission chambers and APRM signals formed as linear sums of selected detectors. It records selected process signals simultaneously with individual LPRM and composite APRM signals.

The ORNL acquisition chain converted and isolated process current loops, maintained signal and ground isolation, used conditioning with filtering and gain, and simultaneously recorded fourteen channels. Short online analysis during constant-power tests was used to evaluate recording quality.

The study uses PSD, cross-PSD, phase difference, and coherence for paired signals, with stated sampling and anti-aliasing settings. It treats coherence as a measure of correlation and reports uncertainty in the coherence estimate.

The study finds that coherence between composite APRM and local LPRM signals depends on both frequency and detector position, with different behavior near the core center and edge in the documented BWR data.

The study warns that unmeasured sensor and conditioning response can affect phase interpretation, and that low coherence can result from instrumentation-lead contamination rather than a real lack of process correlation.

For the documented BWR-4 installation, the study concludes that existing sensor and conditioning signals under normal full-power operation supported noise surveillance to about 1–2 Hz, while only selected process variables showed sufficient coherence with APRM neutron signals for useful monitoring.

The paper argues that fluctuations of neutron-flux and process signals add state information beyond mean values, and identifies real-time spectral monitoring over a broad frequency range as a surveillance objective.

section_path: 2 Digital Frequency Analysis and its Disadvantages
text: The paper relates sampling frequency, anti-alias filtering, record length, bandwidth, and frequency resolution in digital spectral analysis. It highlights the trade-off between low-frequency resolution, high-frequency coverage, computation, and analysis delay.

The described extended frequency analysis low-pass filters and decimates digitized time series to form longer lower-frequency records, allowing multidecade spectral coverage with limited storage while preserving a controlled resolution strategy.
The paper recommends spectral windows for finite time series to reduce sidelobes and describes using overlapping intervals to avoid gaps and improve spectral accuracy.
For the stated method, the analog acquisition requirement is an anti-alias low-pass filter and ADC; subsequent filtered time series and spectra are produced computationally from the digitized signal.
The accuracy test reports that spectral error depends on spectral shape and dynamic range, and that prewhitening may be needed when the signal spectrum spans a large amplitude range.

The paper states that lower-frequency spectra assembled from fewer intervals carry larger statistical errors, and relates relative spectral error to the number of independent averaged intervals and effective window use.
The ORNL study acquired LPRM, APRM, and process-sensor noise signals during normal full-power operation, using several four-hour recordings to obtain sufficient statistical precision.
The study uses coherence as its principal descriptor and reports frequency- and location-dependent relationships between local and average neutron monitors.

The study reports that APRM neutron-noise coherence was significant for selected core-flow, pressure, differential-pressure, and total-steam-flow signals, but negligible for several other process signals and frequency ranges.
The authors conclude that only process variables with sufficient demonstrated correlation to the neutron signal can support useful neutron-signal-based monitoring in the documented BWR configuration.
The reported system learns normal reactor-noise patterns, tracks deviations, and explicitly emphasizes false-alarm-rate control in multivariate surveillance.

The paper distinguishes surveillance, which classifies normal versus abnormal status, from diagnosis, which identifies source and degree. It notes the practical scarcity of abnormal plant patterns and the reliance on independently labeled normal data.

section_path: II Elements of an Autonomous Surveillance System
text: The system separates a learning phase that establishes normal limits from a decision phase that tests whether a signal lies outside those learned regions. It lists neutron noise among measurements conditioned and transformed into classification features.

The study defines a normal training region from vectors assumed to be within design specifications and classifies observations by whether they lie inside a covariance-based boundary; it uses Mahalanobis distance as one criterion.
Training estimates normal-data mean and covariance and may estimate component probability densities; the paper lists histogram, distributional inference, and potential-function approaches.
HFIR evaluation used a normal PSD training set and a controlled rod-perturbation set as abnormal observations; the reported neutron-detector perturbations were below 0.1% of the mean level.
The reported experiment forms PSD-derived feature vectors, estimates normal covariance from the training set, and flags test patterns outside learned bounds.

The study finds that dimensionality reduction can preserve routine-normal classification while distorting abnormal signatures, and recommends preserving non-routine observations in full detail for later diagnostic processing.
The LPRM system provides signals proportional to local neutron flux and comprises stationary in-core detectors plus control-room signal-conditioning equipment.
Each cited LPRM string contains four axially spaced detectors, while channel assignments to APRMs draw from different radial and axial positions to form a representative average-power indication.

The documented detector assembly contains four fission chambers and signal cables at fixed axial spacing, so its readings represent a spatially distributed local-flux measurement rather than one core-wide point measurement.
The detector operates in the ionization region at approximately 100 VDC, and both neutron-induced fission and external gamma radiation can ionize its gas volume.

For the documented power-range LPRM, the detector is continuously exposed and uranium depletion reduces sensitivity; the channel is periodically calibrated with the TIP system. Its output is a small DC current proportional to fission neutron and gamma flux.

The flux amplifier converts detector current to analog voltage and provides selectable gain ranges and adjustment to accommodate detector depletion; its output feeds averaging, rod-block, and process-computer functions.
The documented channel has operate, bypass, and calibration modes. Bypass removes the output from downstream use, while calibration substitutes a calibrator current for the detector input.

The LPRM trip logic compares amplifier output with threshold values; the source states that an upscale trip can indicate either an upscale channel failure or high local neutron flux, while a separate downscale trip is also provided.

The source describes spatially sparse LPRM placement and uses core symmetry to extrapolate readings into uninstrumented locations; coverage and geometry therefore condition the meaning of channel comparisons.
The cited design calibrates LPRMs every six to eight weeks at full power because fission-chamber depletion reduces sensitivity; TIP measurements provide the local reference used for gain adjustment.

LPRM readings feed APRM average-power calculation, local rod-block calculation, calibration through TIP, and process-computer core-performance calculations, demonstrating that one channel can have multiple downstream uses.
The documented LPRM design table reports neutron sensitivity and a nonzero gamma sensitivity, making detector-specific response characteristics relevant when interpreting the recorded current.
The letter describes non-intrusive noise monitoring using instrumentation already present at commercial plants to assess vessel-internal integrity and plant-system behavior.
The NRC framed continuous on-line noise diagnostics as an early-warning mechanism: detecting abnormal signals before failures can enable earlier corrective action.
The program acquired both normal and abnormal neutron signatures and used pattern recognition to establish normal plant signatures before identifying operational deviations.

The planned surveillance architecture included data logging to retain typical sensor signatures for later independent evaluation, and demonstrated stability measurement without external perturbation in the cited BWR work.
In the Sequoyah demonstration, PSDREC learned baseline signatures during normal operation and distinguished abnormal signatures over a two-and-a-half-year continuous measurement series.
Random stationary neutron-noise spectra were tracked more successfully than non-stationary process-noise spectra, with 10% and 20% respectively categorized as suspect in the demonstration.

The continuous record was valuable for separating structural-motion spectral changes from changes associated with boron concentration and fuel burnup; sporadic collection would make those effects difficult to separate.
The Sequoyah measurements combined neutron noise with core-exit thermocouple noise to infer core coolant-flow velocity, illustrating complementary-sensor interpretation.
The source reports reliable two-and-a-half-year operation and buffer-connected use of reactor signals without interfering with plant operation; the demonstration used more than 20 sensor signals.

The NRC letter reports utility use of neutron-noise analysis for core-internal degradation assessment, while noting reluctance to use continuous measurements despite their potential for early detection.

The document identifies incomplete contextual reactor data, such as boron concentration and burnup, as a chief ambiguity in neutron-noise interpretation; cross-correlation with other sensor types can reduce that ambiguity.

The BWR demonstration could not establish a useful baseline because sufficient full-power normal-operation data were unavailable, explicitly showing the dependence of surveillance on normal reference coverage.
The incore system supplies neutron-flux-distribution and selected fuel-outlet-temperature information, but is a data-acquisition system rather than a protective or control function.

Movable fission chambers provide localized flux-distribution data used for hot-channel-factor verification, excore axial-flux-difference calibration, rod-position verification, and quadrant-power-tilt checks.
Fixed core-exit thermocouples complement neutron measurements but their anomalous readings require investigation and are not used for all technical-specification compliance checks.
Movable miniature fission chambers permit detailed core flux mapping and are driven to selected locations, whereas their guide thimbles remain inserted during normal operation.
The drive cable contains a coaxial conductor for transmitting fission-chamber current, and each detector can be routed through a common calibration path for direct detector correlation.
The cited configuration supports spare routing and manual or semiautomatic flux-map control, with separate position displays and power supplies for each detector.
Core-exit temperatures can form a radial power map through enthalpy-rise comparison, but flow mixing creates uncertainty; the source normalizes thermocouples to periodic incore flux-detector data.
The cited fission chamber has specified thermal-neutron and gamma sensitivities and transmits its signal through a coaxial cable threaded through the hollow drive cable.

The system records detector position, selected path, and operating mode, and uses interlocks to prevent path changes unless the detector is withdrawn; these auxiliary states establish measurement context.
Detector-current readout uses selectable ranges and produces recorder and plant-computer outputs; special picoammeter measurement and a low-noise supply are provided for low-level signals.
Calibration scans measure detector output across voltage steps to identify a plateau operating region, after which detectors are normalized for consistent channel-to-channel readings.
Flux mapping records power conditions, detector position, continuous axial profiles, and current/recorder response; the resulting profile is transmitted for later reduction and evaluation.

Movable incore detectors represent actual flux distribution more directly than leakage-dependent excore instruments; the source therefore calibrates excore outputs against incore axial-flux-difference measurements.

The documented incore-excore calibration collects multiple flux distributions during an axial xenon transient, records all excore currents, fits their relationship by linear regression, and adjusts isolation-amplifier gains without changing raw detector current.

The on-line computer receives flux-proportional analog inputs together with detector-selection, path, scan, and record state signals; collection is organized for rapid later reduction and comparison with other online systems.
The mapping program makes repeated nearby readings and compares neighboring points, then normalizes for reactor-power drift, detector differences, scale settings, and low-power leakage current.

The source corrects each pass to a common power level using integrated excore output, establishes detector normalization in a common thimble, applies range and leakage-current corrections, and extrapolates selected locations through core symmetry.
The summary distinguishes movable fission-chamber flux maps, which are collected for computer analysis, from continuously available thermocouple approximations with backup manual readout.
The study analyzes ex-core neutron-detector noise together with reactor-pressure and steam-flow effects across fuel cycles.
Noise measurement was used to characterize principal reactor-parameter patterns and identify sources as part of defining normal-operation stability limits.

Ex-core compensated ion chambers were used for power fluctuation analysis; the amplifier response was flat to 100 Hz, while other measuring-system frequency and phase responses were characterized and corrected.

During stationary full-power operation, the study recorded 14 channels for about six hours and used different spectral averaging counts across two frequency ranges, yielding different stated accuracies.
The source distinguishes globally propagated boiling-related noise from local noise detectable only near a disturbance, and represents detector behavior through normalized PSD, phase, and coherence.
Between 0.01 and 2 Hz the ex-core detectors had equal amplitudes within measurement accuracy and nearly zero phase shift, consistent in this study with global reactivity-driven fluctuations.
The reported global-noise break frequency depends on density-fluctuation velocity and core height; the calculated 1 Hz value agreed with measured neutron-flux PSD behavior for the studied reactor.

The study reports decreasing inter-detector coherence below 1 Hz and attributes the behavior to frequency-dependent detection area and power-feedback effects; it calls the low-frequency derivation qualitative.
A low-frequency neutron-noise peak had high inter-detector coherence and zero phase; comparison with pressure suggested a pressure-induced reactivity oscillation in the documented plant.
The source observed an additional 1.5–5 Hz global term and linked it through coherence and transfer analysis to main-steam-flow oscillations and pressure response.
Within a fuel cycle, PSD and RMS neutron-noise characteristics varied at roughly measurement accuracy during normal operation; the authors propose RMS as supplementary surveillance information.
The conclusions state that noise characteristics can vary between fuel cycles with reactor conditions, and require RMS recalibration at the beginning of each fuel cycle.

In the Fort St. Vrain application, ex-core neutron-noise signals were compared with vessel-displacement probes to infer a predominant movement direction; the result depended on a cross-signal comparison, not on neutron noise alone.

The TMI-2 work used noise-analysis methods for several post-accident assessments, including instrumentation performance and bulk coolant boiling; it illustrates diagnostic application scope beyond a single neutron-current channel.

The report states that assessment of abnormal plant behavior required baseline or reference signatures for normal behavior, because abnormal signatures should be compared against an operational reference.

The authors recommend extending baseline acquisition beyond neutron noise to other signals and to operating conditions other than full power, explicitly treating operating context as part of a usable reference set.
The planned continuous-monitoring system was intended to acquire and catalog selected noise signatures automatically before detecting deviations from baseline conditions.
The report describes stochastic modeling to predict the sensitivity of noise analysis to postulated anomalies, including the minimum detectable in-core boiling through ex-core neutron detectors.
For BWRs, the report identifies neutron-noise applications including void-fraction measurement, in-core component vibration detection, and core-power stability monitoring.

The cited BWR approach estimates decay ratio or similar stability parameters by time-series analysis of power-range neutron-monitor signals, framing the output as a dynamic indicator rather than a causal diagnosis.

The 1983 research review lists PWR pressure-noise assessment, the Sequoyah demonstration, BWR stability assessment from neutron noise, and a study of PWR ex-core neutron-noise sensitivity to fuel elements.
The program combined neutron-noise work with pressure, loose-parts, temperature-noise, and automated-diagnostic studies, establishing a multisignal surveillance scope.
The review records incomplete detailed signature analysis and unavailable high-pressure sensor-line tests, showing that raw signatures require characterization beyond their initial acquisition.
The program added in-core neutron and temperature-noise measurements at Sequoyah-1 and noise measurements at Dresden-2 to its original plan.
SDMS is presented as a proof-of-principle self-diagnostic and prognostic system combining distributed sensors, signal processing, and baseline/degradation trials.
The component-selection process used failure history, consequence and failure rate, laboratory simulation feasibility, and unresolved degradation mechanisms.
The demonstration architecture combines distributed processing nodes, multisensor RF tags, up to 50 sensor inputs, and parallel wired/RF links for fault tolerance.
The report separates sensor-suite and interface verification, integrated commissioning, and formal trials using data for process-model development and database verification.
The ORNL assessment states that no commercial neutron-flux sensor is suitable above 550 °C and identifies high-temperature fission-chamber insulation shorting as a reliability concern.

High temperature and gamma radiation limit electronics, while in-vessel sensor deployment makes cabling, penetrations, communications, and sensor survivability part of the measurement-system constraint.

The assessment treats neutron flux, core temperature, pressure, flow, level, power distribution, and component health as linked monitoring needs, and explicitly includes calibration and maintenance requirements.

For advanced reactors, the assessment prioritizes in-situ calibration and optimized placement that maximizes information while minimizing sensor count; it notes conventional power sensors can burn out in harsh in-core environments.

The study develops and checks a neutron-noise model for two-phase flow against experiment and diffusion calculations. It explicitly limits the model to interpreting the University of Washington reactor experiments rather than claiming general applicability.

The experiment used distant ionization chambers and nearby fission chambers. Far-field detectors responded to the global neutron-field perturbation, whereas near-field detectors contained both global and local components.

The model assumes void-fraction fluctuations drive the observed noise and that a propagating perturbation produces cross-spectrum phase linear in frequency. The authors state this propagation form is exact only under restricted flow assumptions.

For the documented reactor, far-field detector cross-spectra and a characteristic spectral sink supported the point-model description. The authors caution that far-field point-model behavior is not necessarily general beyond that configuration.

Near-field noise is decomposed into global, local and interference components. In the cited experiment, high-frequency phase became linear as the local component dominated, allowing a propagation velocity to be inferred from phase slope.
